title: 128k Long-Context Performance Deep Dive - Aurora Health
topics: KV cache management and eviction strategies
summary: Deep technical session focused on serving 128k+ token workloads for Aurora Health's document ingestion and QA product. Covered KV cache sizing and eviction, chunking/semantic window strategies, batching policies to hit latency SLOs, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed next steps: run a 128k pilot bench on Aurora sample set, share benchmark spreadsheet and SOC2/VPC docs, and follow up on resource sizing for Dedicated/private cluster.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-05 15:00 UTC | Duration 75m | Attendees: Samir Patel, Dana Liu (Redwood)  Maya Thompson, Luis Ortega, Priya Nair (Aurora)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. This is the deep dive on long-context performance for the 128k scenario we talked about. Dana's gonna run the runtime and kernel questions, I'll handle deployment/contract and next steps.
[00:18] Maya: Thanks Samir. Super interested - we ingest large patient record bundles and need to run QA+summarization across entire histories, so the 128k context isn't academic for us, it's production.
[00:30] Dana: Got it. Quick clarification - when you say 128k are you expecting single prompt sequences that are 128,000 tokens or more of combined prompt+history and then generation?
[00:42] Luis: Mostly single query over a concatenated set of documents, yes. Typical generation length is small, like 256 tokens, but the encoder context is the whole record.
[00:54] Dana: Ok that maps to prefix heavy workloads. Two main knobs we look at: KV cache management (we avoid re-encoding prefixes where possible) and chunking / windowing to limit attention.
[01:10] Priya: Security note - Aurora will require VPC + KMS for Private deployments. We also have requirements around audit logs and SSO. We'll share the SOC2 scope later.
[01:25] Samir: That's fine - Redwood Private supports customer-managed networking and KMS/HSM integrations; we'll share the docs after the call.
[01:38] Dana: I'll start with runtime. For 128k context the two common approaches we use with customers are: 1) full long-context model with attention optimizations (FlashAttention, blocked attention, kernel fusion), 2) chunked retrieval with a semantic router + on-the-fly KV stitching. Tradeoffs: full attention gives simpler semantics but needs very high memory and optimized kernels; chunking reduces memory but you need to handle cross-chunk references.
[02:05] Luis: For our workflows, cross-chunk co-references are important - e.g., medication mention in 5th doc referenced in note in 23rd doc - we can't drop cross references casually.
[02:18] Dana: Right. We use an overlap/stride chunker for those cases. Typical config is 32k chunk size with 4k overlap and semantic anchors. For 128k we might do a 32k*4 layout or 16k*8 depending on tokenization. It depends on how many cross references you expect.
[02:39] Maya: What about latency - our SLO is 700ms p95 for the generation step. Is that realistic with a 128k prefix?
[02:50] Dana: For a naive full attention run on a 128k sequence you will be in the multi-second region - often 5-10s depending on model size and hardware. With optimized kernels like FlashAttention2 and streaming KV (we avoid redoing attention for prefix tokens after first pass) we can get that down, but the more reliable path to <1s is chunking + parallel retrieval + local fusion.
[03:12] Samir: Also worth noting Dedicated pools let us pin GPUs and tune batch sizes aggressively; Dedicated customers often hit much better tail latency because of reserved capacity and warmed KV caches.
[03:25] Luis: Any numbers you can share - tokens/sec, memory, GPUs required?
[03:30] Dana: For a 70B model quantized 4-bit on A800 type instances (best case), single-node throughput for full 128k attention before fusion is low - maybe 10-20 tokens/sec with huge memory pressure. Using chunked flow with KV stitching and a two-stage run (encode chunks in parallel, then fuse relevant windows) we've seen effective end-to-end latency drop to ~600-900ms for small generations on tuned Dedicated setups. Those are lab numbers - actual numbers vary by prompt distribution.
[04:01] Maya: What's the role of quantization here? We were told 4-bit can cause hallucination regressions - how much worse is QA accuracy?
[04:12] Dana: Quantization reduces memory and increases throughput, but yes there's a tradeoff with numerics. For QA workloads we recommend starting with 8-bit quant or quant-aware fine tuning for critical paths. For many customers, 4-bit plus small adapter or calibration keeps accuracy within 1-2% for extractive QA, but you should evaluate on your own eval set. Redwood Optimize has a quant recommendation report we can run on your evals.
[04:40] Priya: On the Private side, can we do air-gapped? Our compliance demands that for some facilities.
[04:48] Samir: Yes - our Private offering supports on-prem air-gapped installs. There are tradeoffs on observability retention and remote support, we can provide a hardened bundle and on-site install assistance.
[05:00] Dana: Back to KV - eviction policy matters. For your workload I suspect LRU with semantic pinning for active patient contexts works best. We also provide a tiered KV: hot (GPU RAM), warm (node SSD), cold (object store). Hot cache for the current session, warm layer for recent patients.
[05:24] Luis: How big is hot cache per session typically?
[05:28] Dana: If you encode 128k tokens that can be 30-40GB of KV depending on model. So hot cache for the entire record is expensive. Typical pattern: keep only active and recently accessed segments in hot, prefetch heuristically based on semantic anchors, fall back to warm SSD. That's where latency variability comes from.
[05:49] Maya: Do you have an automatic prefetch policy we can tweak?
[05:53] Dana: Yup - our router supports workload-aware prefetch policies: predictive (model-based), time-based, and explicit hinting from the client. We recommend starting with predictive prefetch based on past access patterns, then add explicit hints from your ingestion pipeline for known hot segments.
[06:10] Luis: Ok. What about batching - we have a concurrent user base of ~3000 active sessions. If we batch aggressively we save cost but increase p95. How do you recommend setting batching thresholds for this mix?
[06:22] Dana: We balance by route. For high SLO routes (interactive UI), we keep max batch size low (like 1-4 requests) and use microbatching with 10-30ms aggregation. For background or overnight jobs we batch to full device capacity. Redwood Dedicated allows separate pools so you can isolate interactive traffic. Also we have dynamic burst pools for spikes.
[06:41] Maya: Does Redwood runtime support per-route SLO config?
[06:44] Samir: Yes - per-route policies, autoscale, and canary rollouts. You can set latency SLOs and Redwood Optimize will suggest batching/cache settings to fit cost/latency targets.
[06:57] Priya: For encryption in motion in VPC mode do you terminate TLS at the customer gateway? We need client side certs.
[07:06] Samir: In Private we can integrate with your TLS termination and mutual TLS. For hosted we provide KMS and transit encryption but not customer TLS termination. We'll include network diagrams in the SOC2 packet.
[07:20] Dana: Another runtime optimization: attention sparsity patterns. For long memory, we often mix local windowed attention for full sequence and global tokens for anchors. That reduces compute from O(n^2) to something closer to n*window + anchors cost and works well for documents with locality.
[07:41] Luis: Are those changes model-level or runtime-level?
[07:44] Dana: Mostly runtime via attention masks - no model re-training needed for sliding window + global tokens if model architecture supports it. For some specialized sparse kernels we see 3-4x perf gains for long sequences.
[07:58] Maya: Sounds promising. What about quantization compatibility with these sparse kernels?
[08:02] Dana: It varies. Some sparse kernels have good support for 8-bit; 4-bit support is improving but you should benchmark. We'll run a compatibility matrix on your model of choice.
[08:16] Luis: Are there any open source equivalents for these optimizations? We're trying to compare engineering effort vs adopting Redwood.
[08:23] Dana: There are OSS projects - FlashAttention, xFormers and some sparse attention libraries - but integrating them reliably across GPU types and productionizing (patches, kernel selection, fallback) is a lot of effort. Redwood's runtime orchestrates kernel selection and fallback automatically.
[08:40] Maya: Let's talk about an experiment. We want a 128k pilot on our UAT data set of 10k patient records. What would you need from us?
[08:49] Samir: We'll need sample tokenized inputs or a representative sample text corpus, an eval set for QA and hallucination checks, and network access if you want on-prem. Ideally a small pass of 100 documents first for smoke.
[09:02] Dana: Also tell us expected concurrency and p95 targets. That informs whether we use Dedicated pilot or Hosted with burst.
[09:10] Luis: Concurrency: 200 interactive, 1k background. p95 interactive: 700ms.
[09:17] Dana: Ok. We'll sketch resource needs but expect Dedicated with 2-4 A800s for stable <1s p95 on tuned chunking; numbers vary by model and quantization.
[09:30] Maya: Any notes on cost impact of keeping hot cache large?
[09:33] Dana: Keeping large hot caches increases GPU count and memory pressure; cost scales with reserved GPU hours. Warm SSD is cheaper but adds latency. Redwood Optimize will produce cost/latency curves for different cache budgets.
[09:48] Priya: About audits - can we get audit logs for model inputs/outputs? There are PHI concerns; we might need redaction.
[09:58] Samir: We can provide audit logs and configurable retention. For PHI we recommend keeping sensitive data encrypted in transit and at rest and applying token-level redaction hooks in your ingestion pipeline. We also support token redaction integrations.
[10:15] Dana: Quick aside on chunk stitching: technique we use is two-pass: encode chunks to KV, run light cross-chunk attention on an anchor subset for global context, then full decode. This reduces quadratic cost. We sometimes use a semantic router to select only top K relevant chunks to fuse.
[10:36] Luis: What's a safe K for accuracy?
[10:39] Dana: Depends - for dense QA maybe K=8-12; for extractive cross-document refs you might need more. We'd recommend experimenting with progressive K and measuring recall on your eval set.
[10:52] Maya: Can we control K at runtime?
[10:54] Dana: Yes - per request hinting is supported. We expose parameters to the SDK.
[11:00] Samir: We'll also share a benchmark sheet. Reference: https://redwood.examples/benchmarks/aurora-128k (note: placeholder link we'll replace with your unique sheet).
[11:12] Priya: One more question - in on-prem air-gapped mode how do you handle kernel updates and security patches?
[11:19] Samir: We provide signed upgrade bundles and can do scheduled maintenance windows. For air-gapped installs we do a secure handoff and provide a patch bundle you can validate via signatures.
[11:32] Dana: Final runtime note: precomputation helps. If you can precompute chunk embeddings and some KV blobs during ingest, real time latency drops significantly.
[11:44] Luis: We'll likely do that.
[11:46] Samir: Ok let's recap and commit next steps.
[11:50] Dana: Cool.
[11:52] End transcript (transcription has occasional mis-labels and auto-generated timestamps may drift).
